Haughty meant to keep his promise to Ugly, yet he still gave the order to kill him. Does a good intention at the start matter, given how it ended? Why or why not?
What were the consequences of Ugly trying to outdo the others with his speech? Could he have chosen differently?
The jackal argued that Ugly would volunteer to be killed if he knew it was for Haughty's sake. Was that a fair argument? Justify your answer.
Haughty had promised to protect Ugly but also had hungry friends who depended on him. Was it right for him to let Ugly be sacrificed, or should his promise have come first? Explain.
Why do you think the lion wanted to keep his friendship with the carpenter separate from his friends the jackal and the crow?
The lion meant to help his hungry friends, but bringing them near the carpenter put his friend in danger. Should we judge the lion by what he meant or by what nearly happened? Why?
What might have happened if the carpenter had trusted the lion's friends and come down from the tree? What does that tell you about the lion's choice?
The carpenter said a person's character can be judged by the company they keep. Was he right to judge the lion by his friends? Give your best reasoning.
How do you think Constance felt when Sprawl kept boasting about being brave?
Sprawl wanted to keep his family safe by staying home. Did his plan turn out the way he hoped? What actually happened?
Sprawl boasted that the ocean could not hurt him. What might have happened if the waves had been much bigger?
What would have happened if Shell-Neck had kept his mouth shut?
The ganders told Shell-Neck exactly what would happen. He spoke anyway. What would have been different if he had listened?
Shell-Neck promised to stay quiet and then spoke. Was he wrong? Should his friends be angry with him?
Shell-Neck broke a promise he meant to keep. Was he foolish, or was it just very hard to stay silent? Have you ever done that?
How do you think Readywit and Fatalist felt when Forethought told them about the fishermen coming?
Forethought left his friends to save himself. Why do you think he made that choice, and was it the right one?
Readywit and Fatalist wanted to stay in their own lake. Did staying keep them safe? What happened instead?
Readywit meant to hide and protect himself, and that partly worked, while Fatalist died. Should their choices be judged by what they intended or by how things ended? Why?
What happened because Fatalist would not leave the lake?
If Fatalist had gone with Forethought, how might the story have ended differently? What does that suggest about thinking ahead?
Fatalist said, 'Why worry?' Do you think he was right to stay? Why?
Was it right for Forethought to leave his friends behind when they would not listen to him? Justify your answer.
How do you think the mother sparrow felt after the elephant broke her nest?
The sparrow wanted revenge for her lost eggs. Why do you think the friends helped her, and was revenge the right reason to act?
The friends wanted to punish the elephant. Did they get what they wanted? How did it turn out?
The woodpecker comforted the sparrow but then helped plan the elephant's death. Were his intentions kind or cruel? Explain.
What happened to the elephant because the friends worked together?
Could the friends have stopped the elephant or protected the nest without killing him? What might that have looked like?
Do you think the friends did the right thing by tricking the elephant? Why?
The friends tricked and killed the elephant to avenge the sparrow's chicks. Was killing the elephant a fair punishment? Give your best reason.
How do you think the old gander felt when the geese would not listen to his warning?
The geese ignored the old gander's warning until they were trapped. Why do you think they did not listen to him?
The geese wanted to keep living in their tree. Did ignoring the warning help them? What happened?
The old gander warned the geese to prevent harm and later saved them. Should we judge him by his warning or by his rescue? Why?
What happened because the geese did not cut down the vine?
What could the geese have done differently when the old gander first warned them? What might have changed?
The old gander told the geese to pretend to be dead. Do you think that was a good plan? Why?
Was it right for the geese to rely on the old gander to save them after they had ignored him? Justify your answer.
How do you think the ram felt when he was lost and all alone in the forest?
The lion first feared the ram and then decided he was weak. Put yourself in the lion's place: why did he change his mind, and was his final judgment fair?
What did the lion want when he attacked the ram? Did he get what he expected?
The lion meant to prove the ram was weak. Did his intention match what actually happened, and why does that gap matter?
What happened because the lion judged the ram by how he looked?
What did the lion's mistake lead to, and what should he have done before attacking?
Do you think the lion was right to be afraid of the ram at first? Why?
The lion reasoned that because the ram ate grass, it must be weak. Was that good reasoning? Why or why not?
How do you think Spike-Ear felt when Smart asked him to give up his body?
Smart told Spike-Ear his plan would help them both. From Spike-Ear's point of view, why was that not really true, and whose view mattered most?
What did Smart say he wanted when he came up with his plan? What actually happened to Spike-Ear?
Smart intended to find food for everyone. Is a good intention enough to excuse what happened to the camel? Why or why not?
Smart's trick made the lion run away. What happened to the camel and to Meat-Face because of that plan?
Follow what Smart's cleverness caused, step by step, from the camel to Meat-Face to the lion. What should Smart have done instead when there was no food?
Spike-Ear said giving his body was 'a good deed.' Do you think he was right? Why?
Spike-Ear trusted Smart because Smart called the plan noble. Was that a strong reason to trust him? What should Spike-Ear have asked first?
Why do you think the people and the king liked the monk so much?
The monk seemed wise to everyone. If you were the king, what question would you have asked to test him before trusting him?
What did the monk want when he told the king he could read thoughts and visit heaven?
The monk claimed to visit heaven and the king believed him. Did the king get what he expected, and whose intention was dishonest?
What happened to the king because he believed the monk?
What were the consequences of the king trusting the monk without proof, and what should he have done sooner?
Counselor Strong said the king was 'being foolish.' Do you think he was right? Why?
Strong's plan was to burn the monk's body to find the truth. Was that a fair way to test him? Why or why not?
How do you think the wife felt when she first saw that her baby was a snake?
The neighbors said to throw the snake away, but the mother kept him. Whose feelings should decide what happens to a child, and why?
What did Godly want when he set out on his long journey?
Godly loved his wife and went to find a bride for a snake. Did he expect anyone to say yes? What did he actually get?
What happened when people saw the beautiful girl with the snake?
The girl chose to marry the snake even though everyone objected. What might have happened if she had listened to her relatives, and why did she not?
The girl said she would be like Blossom. Do you think that was a good reason to marry the snake? Why?
The girl said her decision was not up for discussion. Was she right to refuse to explain her choice? Why or why not?
How do you think the gods felt when Blossom died even after they tried to save him?
The gods tried hard to protect Blossom. If you were one of the gods, how would you explain to Blossom why he still died?
What did the gods want when they asked Yama to spare Blossom?
The gods wanted to save Blossom, yet he still died. What did they expect, and did their good intention change anything?
What happened to the gods' plan to save Blossom?
Each god passed the decision to the next, from Yama to Time to Death. What did that chain lead to, and could anyone have changed it?
Yama said Blossom's death was his fate. Do you think that is a fair answer? Why?
Yama said it was not his decision and that Time decides. Was that a good enough reason to let Blossom die? Why or why not?
How do you think Red-Face felt when Needle-Face kept telling him he was wrong?
What did Needle-Face want when she flew down to the monkeys? Did she get what she hoped for?
What happened because Red-Face would not listen? Who got hurt?
Red-Face grabbed Needle-Face instead of listening to her. What do you think he was feeling in that moment?
How do you think Right-Mind felt when the money was gone and his friend blamed him?
Wrong-Mind said he wanted to divide the money fairly. What did he really want?
What happened to the money after the friends buried it, and who was hurt by Wrong-Mind's plan?
Wrong-Mind's father said, 'This is a bad plan.' How do you think the father felt about helping his son?
The heron was so sad he went to the pond and cried. How do you think he was feeling, and what do you think he hoped the crab would do?
The crab meant to help the herons, but his plan made things worse. How do you think the herons felt about the crab's help?
The herons did exactly what the crab said. What do you think might have happened if they had asked someone else for help instead?
Was the crab a good helper? Tell me why you think so.
Did Naduk plan to take Lakshman's son, or did he decide suddenly?
Naduk only took the boy after Lakshman lied about the beam. Did Naduk plan his revenge in advance?
Lakshman told a lie about the mice. Was Naduk right to tell a lie back?
Lakshman lied first. Does someone else's lie make your own lie all right? Why or why not?
Naduk lied to teach Lakshman a lesson. Was he punishing him, or just getting even? Is there a difference?
The two parrots were brothers, but one was cruel and one was kind. How do you think each parrot felt about the way it had been raised?
The first parrot scared the king and the second parrot welcomed him. Did either parrot really mean to help or hurt the king?
The second parrot was cared for by a kind holy man. What do you think would have happened if the first parrot had been raised in the hermitage too?
The first parrot shouted cruel words at the king. Was it fair to blame the parrot for what it had been taught? Tell me why.
The thief joined the group to steal the gems. How do you think he felt when he saw his new friends in danger?
The thief planned to hurt the travelers, but in the end he saved them. Did he act the way you expected him to?
What do you think might have happened if the thief had thought only about himself?
The chief trusted the bird's song and almost cut the travelers open. Was the chief right to trust the bird? Tell me what you think.
The monkey thought it was protecting the king when it struck the bee. Why do you think it did not understand what it was really doing?
The monkey meant to help, yet the king died. Do you think the monkey was responsible for the king's death? Explain.
The king appointed a foolish monkey as his sword-bearer. What should he have thought about before making that choice?
The queen called the monkey a fool who repaid trust with treachery. Was she right to blame the monkey, or should the king share the blame? Give your reasons.
The story says we should keep a safe distance from those who lack sense. But the king was the monkey's friend. Is it wrong to befriend someone who does not think things through?
Swift warned the birds but Gay-Neck ignored him. Why do you think Gay-Neck decided the food was worth the risk?
Swift meant to protect the birds, yet they were still caught. Did Swift fail, or was he right to warn them? Explain.
Gay-Neck's plan only worked because every dove pulled together. What might have happened if only a few of them had tried to fly away?
Was Gay-Neck right to ignore Swift's warning? Give your reasons.
The two necks belonged to the same bird. How do you think the first neck and the second neck each felt about the nectar?
The second neck wanted to teach the first neck a lesson. Did it get what it wanted in the end?
What do you think might have happened if the first neck had shared the nectar?
The second neck thought it was right to punish the first neck. Do you agree? Tell me why.
Crop-Ear was so worried about the mouse that he forgot about his guest. How do you think Wide-Bottom felt?
Crop-Ear wanted to keep his food safe, but he hurt his friend's feelings instead. Did he get what he wanted?
What do you think might have happened if Crop-Ear had told Wide-Bottom about the mouse right away?
Wide-Bottom grew angry because he thought Crop-Ear did not care about him. What was Crop-Ear actually feeling, and why did it look so different to his guest?
Crop-Ear meant to be a good host, yet he drove his guest away. In this story, was his intention or the outcome more important? Explain.
Wide-Bottom looked for the mouse's hole instead of just the mouse. Why does finding the cause of a problem matter more than chasing the problem itself?
How do you think the Brahman felt when his wife told him he should be ashamed?
Why do you think the Brahman's wife was so bitter, even though the Brahman only wanted to help others?
The Brahman wanted to give a gift even though he had little. What do you think he hoped would happen?
The Brahman meant well, but his wife disagreed. Should we judge his plan by what he meant to do, or by how his wife felt about it?
What might happen if the Brahman went to the village and no one gave him anything?
The Brahman said a little help at the right time is good. What could go wrong if you give at the wrong time?
The Brahman said even a little help is good. Do you agree? Tell why.
The wife said giving to a poor Brahman is pointless. Was she right? Give a reason for your answer.
Red-Face wanted to shoot the boar and eat its meat. Did things turn out the way he wanted? Why or why not?
Both Red-Face and the jackal had plans they thought were good. Why did their intentions lead to such bad outcomes?
The jackal said he would eat slowly. What would have happened if he really had eaten slowly?
Whose mistake caused more harm, the hunter's or the jackal's? Explain how each one's choice led to the ending.
How do you think the son felt when his father threw him out for buying the book?
Why do you think Ocean cared so much about the hundred rupees, even though his son found the book valuable?
Ocean wanted his son to make money. Did throwing him out help the son in the end?
Ocean meant to teach his son a lesson, but the son became crown prince. Was the outcome what Ocean intended? Explain.
What might have happened if the prince HAD gone to visit the princess at night?
The prince followed the book's warning and stayed away. How did that choice change what happened to Mister Duly?
Mister Duly says, 'What's duly his, a man receives.' Do you think that is fair? Tell why.
Was it right for the king to make Mister Duly the crown prince? Give a reason for your answer.
Mister Duly got his rewards partly through luck and other people's mistakes. Is it right that he received so much? Argue for or against.
How do you think Soft's wife felt when he said he would leave for Growing City?
Soft's wife believed fate decides how much wealth a person has. Why do you think she wanted him to stay instead of trying to earn more?
Soft worked hard to earn money. Did hard work alone get him what he wanted?
Soft's plan was to earn money by hard work, but his money kept vanishing. What does this story say about plans and their results?
What happened each time Soft stopped to rest in the forest? Why do you think it kept happening?
Soft kept repeating the same journey and lost his money each time. What should he have done differently after the first loss?
Soft said money would make him look important. Do you agree that money makes a person important? Tell why.
The figure said money is worthless if you can't enjoy or share it. Was Soft wrong to still ask for it? Give reasons.
How do you think Greedy felt after following Hang-Ball for 15 years and getting nothing?
Greedy's wife kept pushing him to follow the bull. Why do you think she was so sure it was worth it?
Greedy's wife wanted good food for them. Did following Hang-Ball give them what she wanted?
The she-jackal meant to get easy food, but they wasted 15 years. Was the plan sensible from the start? Explain.
What did Greedy and his wife lose by following Hang-Ball for so long?
Greedy ignored his own doubt and listened to his wife. How did that choice lead to the ending?
Greedy said it was better to stay and eat mice. Do you think he was right? Tell why.
The story says we waste time chasing things that may never happen. Was Greedy's wife wrong to call him lazy? Argue your view.
How do you think the mice felt when the big elephants came through their homes?
The elephants did not mean to hurt the mice. Does it matter that they did not mean it? Why?
The mice asked the elephants to go another way instead of fighting. Was that a good choice?
The mice were angry but asked politely. Why do you think asking worked better than fighting would have?
How do you think Spot felt while he lived with the prince, even though he was treated well?
The prince treated Spot kindly, but Spot was still unhappy. Why do you think good treatment was not enough for Spot?
The prince wanted to keep Spot as a pet. Did that make Spot happy? Why or why not?
The prince meant to be kind to Spot, yet Spot was miserable. What does this tell us about good intentions?
The friends made a plan to save the turtle. What would have happened if the plan had not worked?
The friends' plan worked because each one did a different job. Why was it important that they acted as a team?
Red-Eye warned the king that the crow was sly, but no one listened. How do you think Red-Eye felt as he finally flew away from the cave?
Live-Strong let the owls feed him and trust him while he planned to destroy them. Did he mean them harm from the very first day, or only when he lit the fire? Does it matter which?
Trace what happened step by step, from the day Cloudy threw Live-Strong out to the day the cave burned. Where, if anywhere, could the owls have stopped it?
The crows tricked and killed the owls to win back their tree. Was tricking an enemy that way the right thing to do, or should they have fought openly? Give your reasons.

The owls had killed many crows, and Cloudy's counselors offered peace, war, retreat, a fort, or an alliance. Was cunning the right choice, even though it killed every owl? What else could he have done?
How do you think the owl felt when the crow said he was ugly and mean?
The birds welcomed the crow as the wisest and asked his opinion. Why do you think they trusted him so quickly?
What might happen to the birds if they had two kings at the same time?
The crow warned that two kings would cause trouble. What problems could come from having two leaders?
The crow said the owl was not a good choice. Do you think that was a fair thing to say? Tell why.
Was the crow right to speak up against the owl, even though the birds had already chosen him? Give reasons.
How do you think the rabbits felt when the elephants came and played in their lake?
Why do you think Four-Tusk believed Victory so easily? Put yourself in Four-Tusk's place.
Victory told a lie to save the rabbits. How did that turn out for Four-Tusk and the elephants?
Victory meant to save the rabbits, but he tricked Four-Tusk to do it. Does a good result make the trick right?
What happened to Four-Tusk because he listened to Victory?
If Four-Tusk had asked more questions before touching the water, how might the story have ended differently?
Victory said Four-Tusk should have known he was doing wrong. How do you think Four-Tusk felt when he heard that?
Four-Tusk said, 'I didn't know it was wrong.' Is that a good excuse? Why or why not?
How do you think the partridge felt when he came home and found Speedy living in his nest?
Speedy was scared of Curd-Ear from the very start. Why do you think the partridge didn't believe him? Put yourself in the partridge's place.
Curd-Ear said kind words but did a cruel thing. How did his kind words make the partridge and Speedy feel?
Curd-Ear spoke about kindness but ate them both. Can good words come from a bad heart? What does the story tell us?
What happened to the partridge and Speedy when they trusted Curd-Ear?
What might have happened if the partridge and Speedy had chosen a different judge, or settled the case themselves?
Do you think the partridge or Speedy had the better claim to the nest? Tell how you feel about it.
Speedy said a home belongs to whoever occupies it. Was that a fair rule to use? Why or why not?
How did Friendly feel each time a stranger told him the goat was a different animal?
Why do you think the same kind of lie worked on Friendly three times? Put yourself in his shoes.
The rogues pretended to help by telling Friendly he was wrong. What did they really want?
The rogues sounded like they were correcting him, but they meant to steal the goat. Does a helpful-sounding intention make the trick better or worse?
What happened to the goat because Friendly listened to the strangers?
If Friendly had trusted his own eyes and kept walking, what would have happened to the goat and the rogues?
Friendly kept getting angry at the strangers. Do you think it would have been better to stay calm? How do you feel about it?
Should Friendly have blamed the strangers or himself for losing the goat? Why?
How do you think Haughty felt when the ants kept stinging him and he could not escape?
Haughty was much bigger than the ants, yet he lost. Why do you think that happened? Put yourself in Haughty's place.
Haughty wanted to take a shortcut through the hole. How did that choice turn out for him?
Haughty meant to save time with the shortcut. Did his plan turn out the way he expected? Why or why not?
What happened to Haughty because he got stuck in the hole?
Could Haughty have survived if he had not tried the shortcut, or if he had escaped sooner? Explain.
How do you think the son felt when he saw the single gold coin in the saucer?
Why do you think the son believed the snake had a treasure? Put yourself in his place.
The son wanted all the coins, but he hit the snake. What happened because of that?
Did the son's greed lead to the result he expected? What does the story say about wanting more?
What happened to the Brahman's family after the son hit the snake?
If the son had kept bringing the milk kindly like his father, how would the story have ended?
The Brahman said we should be kind to all living things. Do you think the son was being kind? How do you feel about it?
Was the Brahman right to keep giving milk after his son died? What would you have done, and why?
How do you think the golden bird felt when the swans told him he could not stay?
Why do you think the swans were unwilling to share the lake with the golden bird? Put yourself in their place.
The golden bird wanted to live at the lake. What happened after he complained to the king?
The golden bird meant to get the swans in trouble. Did it turn out the way he wanted? Why or why not?
What happened to the swans when the king told his soldiers what to do?
If the swans had let the golden bird stay, how might the story have ended instead?
Do you think the king was fair to the swans? Tell how you feel about his order.
The king ordered the swans killed, then realized he was wrong. Should a king's orders be obeyed even when they seem unfair? Why?
Put yourself in the fowler's place. Why do you think the dove's song moved him so deeply?
The fowler meant only to shelter from the storm, yet he left changed. Was the outcome what he intended, and what does that suggest?
The dove gave his life to save the fowler. What consequences did that choice have for the dove, his wife, and the fowler?
Was the dove right to sacrifice himself for a man who had killed so many birds? Justify your answer.
The dove owed kindness to a guest, but that guest had caused great harm to birds. Should he have helped his enemy? Why or why not?
How do you think the young wife felt when the thief came into the house?
Why do you think the young wife hugged her husband that night, and how might she have felt about it the next morning?
The old man wanted to thank the thief. Did that turn out the way he expected?
The old man believed the thief helped him. Was the thief's visit really good for him, or did it only seem that way?
What might have happened if the old man had killed the thief?
What would have happened if the old man had killed the thief instead of thanking him?
Was it right for the old man to let the thief go? Tell us why you think so.
Hook-Nose said they should not kill the thief because he helped them. Was that good advice? Give your reasons.
How do you think Ugly-Mug felt when her father gave her away to the prince?
How do you think the prince felt when his own kingdom could not cure him?
King Gift meant to punish Ugly-Mug by giving her away. Did it turn out badly for her?
King Gift gave Ugly-Mug away to punish her. Did his plan work the way he wanted? Why or why not?
What might have happened if Ugly-Mug had not helped the prince?
What would have happened to the prince if no one had overheard the snakes' plan?
How do you think the wife felt when she stubbed her toe in the dark?
What do you think the wife was thinking and feeling as she invented her story about the goddess?
The carpenter hid under the bed to test his wife. What did he think he would find, and what did he find instead?
The carpenter tested his wife to learn the truth. Did he actually learn it, and what did he end up believing?
What might have happened if the wife had told the truth?
What might have happened if the carpenter had punished his wife and the lover instead of praising them?
How do you think the mouse-girl felt about being turned into a girl?
How do you think the girl felt each time she met a new suitor, and why did she keep saying no?
The parents wanted the very best husband for her. Did they get what they wanted?
Yajnavalkya searched for the greatest possible husband for his daughter. Did his plan lead where he expected?
What might have happened if she had married the sun or the wind?
What would have happened if Yajnavalkya had refused to turn her back into a mouse?
How do you think the bird felt when it was caught in the trap?
How do you think the hunter felt when he saw the golden poop, and how did that feeling change what he chose to do?
The hunter meant to keep the bird. Did things turn out the way he planned?
Everyone in this story tried to do the smart thing. Did their intentions lead to the outcomes they wanted?
What might have happened if the king had kept the bird in the cage?
What would have happened if the bird had been kept? Would anyone have learned the truth about its gold?
Every animal guessed a different reason why Curd-Face ran away. Why did they guess differently?
Red-Eye's guess and Live-Strong's guess said more about them than about Curd-Face. Why do people guess differently about the same thing?
Was Live-Strong trying to help the others, or to get rid of his own enemies?
Live-Strong said he wanted to help. How can you tell the difference between helping and using people for your own plan?
How do you think Water-Foot felt about Slow-Poison, and how did that feeling change over the course of the story?
Slow-Poison's plan was to get food without effort. Did his intention match what actually happened?
What were the consequences of Water-Foot trusting Slow-Poison, and who paid the price?
Water-Foot suggested that Slow-Poison should eat the plebeian frogs. Was that a good decision? Justify your answer.
The frogs benefited at first from riding the snake, yet Slow-Poison was deceiving them the whole time. Was Slow-Poison fully to blame, or did the frogs share some of it?
Did Ugly-Mug mean to trick his friend Red-Face?
Ugly-Mug loved Red-Face like a brother, but his wife pushed him. Does why he did it change what he did?
Red-Face trusted Ugly-Mug completely. Was it wrong to trick a friend?
Is betraying a friend who trusts you worse than betraying a stranger? Why?
Ugly-Mug loved his wife and his friend, and both mattered to him. He could not please both. What should he have done?
How do you think Theodore felt when Handsome ate his son?
How do you think Theodore felt about his own plan once Handsome began eating his family?
Theodore wanted to get rid of his relatives. Did his plan work out the way he hoped?
Theodore tried to solve one problem by inviting Handsome in. Did his intention produce the outcome he wanted?
What might have happened if Theodore had never invited the snake into the well?
What were the consequences of Theodore trusting a more powerful animal, and who suffered most?
Was it right for Theodore to ask the snake for help? Tell us why you think so.
Was Theodore's plan to use Handsome against his relatives justified? Give your reasons.
Theodore's relatives were cruel to him, yet he had them eaten. Does their cruelty justify his choice? Why or why not?
When Dusty brought Flop-Ear to the injured lion, what do you think Flop-Ear believed was going to happen? Why did he trust Dusty so easily?
Dusty meant to help the lion get food, but he also tricked a trusting donkey. Was Dusty's plan good, kind, or neither? What makes you say so?
What were the consequences of Flop-Ear trusting Dusty's promise of green grass and friendly she-donkeys? Could Flop-Ear have done anything to avoid that ending?
The lion said he would not be like Flop-Ear. Was the lion right to blame Flop-Ear for being fooled? Give your best reason for or against.
Dusty was loyal to the lion but betrayed Flop-Ear. Which mattered more - loyalty to his master or honesty to a stranger? Why do you think that?
How do you think the potter felt when the king gave him gifts and called him a hero? Why did he feel that way?
Why do you think the king believed the potter was a hero just because of his scar? What did the king want to be true?
The potter wanted to stay in the army. Do you think what happened to him was fair? Why or why not?
The potter was punished even after he offered to prove his bravery in battle. Was the king right to send him away? Give your strongest reason.
What happened because the potter told the truth about his scar? What do you think he should do next?
What did the potter's one honest answer cost him? What might have happened if he had kept lying instead?
How do you think the jackal cub felt when he learned he was not really a lion? Why did he get so angry at his brothers?
The lioness raised the jackal out of pity, but it ended with him threatening his brothers. Did her kindness lead to a good or a bad outcome? Explain.
What were the consequences of the jackal cub growing up believing he was a lion? Who was hurt by that belief?
The lioness told the cub the truth only when he threatened his brothers. Was that the right time to tell him? Why or why not?
Was it right for the lioness to raise a jackal as her own child? What did she owe the cub, and what did she owe her own twins?
How do you think the Brahman felt when his wife asked to bring the cripple along with them? What did he want to happen?
Why did the Brahman agree to bring the cripple along, even though it likely upset him? What was he hoping for?
The Brahman wanted to be kind. Do you think being kind was a good choice here? What happened because of it?
The Brahman gave half his life to save a wife who later betrayed him. Was that a good decision? Give your strongest reason either way.
The wife took the Brahman's money and used up his life. What happened to her in the end because of her choices?
The wife was punished only when the Brahman demanded back what was his. What does that tell you about how her greed finally caught up with her?
How do you think King Joy felt when he let his wife ride on his back? Why did he do it?
Why do you think both King Joy and Splendor gave in to their wives' silly demands? What were they each afraid of?
Splendor shaved his head to make his wife happy. Do you think that was a good way to fix things? What else could he have done?
Splendor said he would do what his wife asked but did not really mean it. Was the trouble he got into his own fault? Give your best reason.
What happened at the end because Splendor said something he did not really mean? What was the result?
What did Splendor's careless words cost him? If he had stayed silent instead, how might the outcome have been different?
How do you think the donkey felt while wearing the tiger-skin and eating all the barley he wanted? Why?
Why did Clean-Cloth think the tiger-skin was a good idea? What did he expect the farmers to believe when they saw the donkey?
Clean-Cloth wanted to feed his hungry donkey. Was the trick a good way to do it? What happened because of it?
Clean-Cloth wanted to help his donkey, but the donkey ended up dead. Was Clean-Cloth responsible for that, or was it only the donkey's fault? Explain.
What happened to the donkey when the farmers heard him bray? Why did the trick stop working?
What were the consequences of the donkey forgetting he was disguised? What could Clean-Cloth have done to prevent it?
How do you think the farmer's wife felt at home that made her want to leave? What did she want most?
Why do you think the farmer's wife believed the rogue so quickly? What made his story about his dead wife sound convincing to her?
The wife thought taking the money to the rogue was a good idea. Was it a good idea? What happened because of it?
The wife blamed bad luck for her misfortune. Was she simply unlucky, or did her own choices cause it? Give your strongest reason.
The rogue took the money and left the wife alone. What happened to her because she trusted him?
What were the consequences of the wife's decision to run away with a stranger? Could she have seen the danger earlier?
Supersmart flatters the lion and frightens the tiger to win the elephant for himself. How do you think the lion and the tiger each felt afterward, and did either of them realize he had been tricked?
Supersmart only wanted food, yet his trick sent the tiger running away in fear. Was he responsible for the tiger's fright even though he never harmed him?
If Supersmart had simply shared the elephant instead of tricking the other animals, what might have happened to him? Which choice would have led to a better outcome?
Supersmart says intrigue is the best way to get what you want. Do you agree that trickery is a good way to solve a problem? What else could he have done?
The moral says a trickster may outsmart his enemies but not his equals. Is being clever the same as being wise? Should Supersmart be admired or blamed for what he did?
Spot missed his home even though the new city had better food. How do you think he felt when he finally came back to his family?
Spot's family was eager to hear about his trip. Why do you think he told them honestly about the good food but also about the mean men, instead of only the good parts?
Spot went abroad hoping to find food, but the big dogs hurt him instead. Did Spot do something wrong, or did things just turn out badly?
Spot left home to escape hunger, yet he met danger abroad. Was leaving the right decision even though it ended badly, or did the outcome prove it was a mistake?
If Spot had stayed home during the famine, what do you think would have happened to him? Was going away worth it?
The story says it is better to appreciate what you have. If Spot had known how his journey would end, what should he have done differently, and what would the consequences have been?
Jewel was so sad about losing his money that he wanted to stop eating. What do you think he was feeling, and why did the dream give him hope?
In court the barber blamed Jewel for what he did. From the barber's point of view, did Jewel share any blame for the monks' deaths? Why or why not?
Jewel only meant to test his dream, but the barber used his idea to hurt many monks. Was Jewel's action still wrong if he never meant for anyone to get hurt?
Jewel struck a monk and it became gold; the barber copied him and killed many monks. How much should Jewel be blamed for an outcome he did not intend?
What do you think the barber should have thought about before he clubbed the monks? What did he forget to consider?
If the barber had stopped to think about what might go wrong, what should he have predicted? What does his mistake teach about acting on someone else's example?
The judges said the barber's act was wrong. Do you think that was a fair decision? Why?
The judges punished only the barber, not Jewel. Was that just? Give a reason for who you think was truly responsible.
The mother had always feared the mungoose might harm her baby. How do you think that fear shaped how she saw his bloody mouth, and did the mungoose understand why she acted as she did?
The mother meant to protect her child, but she killed the loyal mungoose who had just saved him. Was she responsible for his death even though her intention was to keep her baby safe?
If the mother had paused to look inside the house before throwing the jar, what would she have seen, and how would the story have ended?
The story calls her action thoughtless. Was killing the mungoose a fair punishment for what she believed he had done? Give a reason for your view.

The mother loved both the baby and the mungoose. When she saw the blood, her fear for her baby and her trust in the mungoose pulled her in opposite directions. Was she wrong to let fear win over affection?
The four friends all wanted to escape poverty, yet the wheel-bearer warned they had gone too far. How do you think the gold-finder felt when he realized his friend had ignored his warning?
The Brahmans meant only to find enough treasure to live well, but their pursuit led them to a terrible place. Were they responsible for their own suffering even though they intended no harm?
The friends stopped at copper, then silver, then gold, always wanting more. What do you think would have happened if they had stopped at the gold and gone home?
The story says scholarship is less than sense. Do you agree that common sense matters more than knowledge? Justify your answer with something from the story.
The Brahmans were poor, and wanting a better life is not wrong, yet their pursuit of treasure brought disaster. Where is the line between a reasonable wish and dangerous greed?
The wise friend was told he could not share the money and might have to go home. How do you think he felt being left out by his friends?
The three learned friends looked down on the one they called unlearned. From the wise friend's point of view, why do you think he still stayed with them on the journey?
The friends only wanted to show how clever they were, but the lion killed them. Did they mean for anyone to be hurt? Does that make it less bad?
The three friends intended to show off their knowledge, not to cause death. Were they still responsible for what happened, and why?
The wise friend climbed the tree before the lion came to life. What do you think would have happened to him if he had not climbed up?
If the friends had listened to the wise one's warning, what do you think would have happened next, and what does their choice not to listen reveal about them?
The wise friend warned the others but they laughed at him. Do you think he should have tried harder to stop them? Why?
Was the wise friend right to save only himself by climbing the tree, or should he have done more to stop his friends? Justify your choice.
Single-Wit's friends thought they were too clever to be caught. How do you think they felt when the nets came and Single-Wit was already gone?
Thousand-Wit was sure his cleverness could save everyone. Why do you think he refused to listen when Single-Wit said they should flee?
The friends meant to save themselves with their clever plans, but they were caught anyway. Did they do something wrong, or were they just unlucky?
Hundred-Wit and Thousand-Wit intended to protect everyone with their wits, yet they were caught. Should they be blamed for their own fate, or was it simply bad luck?
If Hundred-Wit and Thousand-Wit had left the pond with Single-Wit, what do you think would have happened to them?
What consequence did the two clever fish fail to foresee when they chose to stay? What should that have told them about trusting only their cleverness?
Single-Wit left without his friends even though they were scared too. Was that a fair choice? Why do you think so?
Single-Wit escaped but his friends did not. Should he have done more to convince them to come, or was it right to save himself and his wife? Give your reasoning.
How do you think the jackal felt when Prig sang even after being warned? What did Prig want to happen?
The jackal warned Prig again and again, then reluctantly stayed by the hedge as Prig sang. Whose point of view do you understand better, Prig's or the jackal's, and why?
Prig wanted to sing and thought it would be nice. What actually happened? Did Prig mean to get caught?
Prig meant no harm -- he only thought his voice was beautiful. Was the trouble his fault anyway? Why or why not?
What happened after Prig started to sing? What could Prig have done differently to stay safe?
Prig forgot the pain as soon as the mortar was on his neck. What does that tell you about how he thought about consequences?
The jackal warned Prig many times. Was the jackal right to give advice? How would you have said it differently?
Was the jackal right to say 'Well done' when Prig was caught? What is the difference between a fair warning and mocking someone?
How do you think the fairy felt when Slow came with an axe? What did the fairy want?
Slow's wife and the barber gave very different advice. Whose point of view do you understand better, and why?
Slow wanted to be rich and make more cloth. What actually happened to him? Did he mean for that to happen?
Slow asked for a wish intending to make more cloth, but it led to his death. Can a good intention still cause terrible harm? Explain.
Slow's wife told him what to ask for. What happened next? What should Slow have thought about first?
Slow asked for extra arms and a head but never thought about how people would see him. What consequence did he miss?
Was the barber's advice good or bad? Why do you think the barber told Slow not to ask his wife?
Was it right for Slow to ignore the barber's warning about his wife? What makes a piece of advice worth trusting?
How do you think Seedy felt when he saw the spilled barley-meal? What did he want most in his dream?
In his dream Seedy pictured himself getting angry at his wife. What does that show about how he imagined his future?
Seedy only wanted to imagine being rich. What actually happened to his jar? Did he mean to break it?
Seedy did not intend to kick the jar -- it happened while he dreamed. Is he still responsible for the loss? Why?
What happened because Seedy kept dreaming instead of sleeping? What could he have done to keep the meal safe?
Seedy's daydream grew step by step until it ended in a kick. How did each small wish make the next one bigger?
Seedy's friends laughed at him. Was that fair? What would you say to Seedy?
Was Seedy simply foolish, or just human for dreaming? What is the difference between a harmless dream and a harmful one?
The monkeys laughed at the chief's warning while he clearly saw the danger. Why could they not see what he saw?
The chief monkey only wanted to save everyone, yet he later caused the king's death. Can good intentions lead to destruction?
Trace how the ram's habit led to the deaths of the horses and then the monkeys. Where could the chain have been broken?
Was the chief monkey right to leave the palace instead of staying to protect the others? Justify your answer.
The chief monkey avenged his household by tricking the king into being eaten. Was revenge the right response to his grief?
The fiend feared a rival named Twilight who may not have existed at all. Why did his own fear make him act so strangely?
The thief meant only to steal a horse, and the fiend meant only to spy. Why did both end up fleeing in terror?
The fiend's fear set off a chain: disguise, whip, fall, banyan tree. What could he have done to stop that chain early?
Was the monkey right to tell the fiend to eat the harmless man? Justify what makes that advice dangerous.
The fiend was powerful but was defeated by his own doubts. Is fear a fair punishment for someone who only wanted love?
The Brahman was terrified but stayed calm enough to ask about Cruel's feet. What do you think was going on in his mind?
Cruel intended to keep the Brahman, and the Brahman intended only to be free. Why did the Brahman's plan succeed while Cruel's failed?
What would have happened if Cruel had never made his vow to wash his feet? How did one rule decide the whole outcome?
Was the Brahman right to trick Cruel, or should he have tried to reason with him? Justify your choice.
How do you think Red-Face felt when he could no longer walk? What did he want from Numskull?
Numskull kept giving and Red-Face kept eating. Whose point of view do you understand better, and why?
Numskull wanted to be kind. What actually happened to his fruit? Did he mean to lose it all?
Numskull meant to be generous, but his giving caused harm. Can kindness ever be a mistake? Explain.
What happened because Red-Face ate so much? What could Numskull have done sooner to stop it?
Numskull gave fruit every day without a plan. How did each day's small gift add up to a big loss?
Was Numskull right to keep giving fruit? Why or why not? What would you have told him?
Was Red-Face to blame for eating, or was Numskull, who kept offering? Justify who should have acted differently.
